clue.text: Dine chez Uriah

blocks.note: surface reading: have dinner at the home of someone called Uriah
setter's reading: Uriah Heep in Dickens's David Copperfield, forever protesting how 'umble he is, so dining with him means a meal of humility

explanation.surface: An invitation to dinner at the house of a man named Uriah.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep is the fawning clerk in David Copperfield whose catchphrase is that he is 'very umble'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to apologise abjectly and accept humiliation, which is the dish a host famous for humility would serve.

clue.text: Track-pate? Easily could be

blocks.note: surface reading: a head that could easily be traced or followed
setter's reading: a head shaped and bald like an egg would crack easily, and the printed 'Track' is very likely a misprint for 'Crack'

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Track' as 'Crack': a crackpate is a crackpot, and an egg-shaped head is exactly the kind that cracks easily.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for an intellectual, originally mocking a bald, dome-shaped head like a shell of an egg.

clue.text: Greet glassily, crisply ?

definitions.note: an adverb cluing a noun or verb: bread made crisp

blocks.note: first meaning: salute someone by raising a glass and drinking
second meaning: bread browned under heat until crisp

explanation.surface: Someone says hello in a cold, glassy and clipped manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinking to someone's health is a verb sense; grilled bread made crunchy is the familiar breakfast sense.

clue.text: Rare as a Shakespearian tress was not

definitions.text: as a Shakespearian tress was not

blocks.note: first meaning: of meat, lightly cooked

blocks.clueFragment: as a Shakespearian tress was not
blocks.note: second meaning, cryptic: Shakespeare's heroines' tresses were elaborately dressed and bound up, never left loose under their coifs

explanation.surface: Something unusual, the way a lock of hair in Shakespeare was not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rare' tempts as 'uncommon', but here it is the kitchen sense for steak; the second half plays on hair being done or undone.
explanation.definitionFit: Steak served rare has been cooked only briefly, leaving it short of being properly cooked through.

clue.text: A go like this gives one quite a turn

blocks.note: surface reading: an attempt of this kind; setter's reading: the letter A placed in front of the solution
setter's reading: the result is a word for a turn, the kind a soldier makes on the parade ground when ordered to face the other way

explanation.surface: A particular attempt at something leaves a person startled.
explanation.walkthrough: Put A in front of the answer to get ABOUT, which is a turn, as in a soldier's about-turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A spell of fighting or activity, such as a boxing round, is one go at it.

clue.text: It can get you down, too

definitions.text: It can get you down, too

blocks.clueFragment: It can get you down, too
blocks.note: surface reading: something depressing as well as everything else
setter's reading: a machine that carries people downwards as well as upwards

explanation.surface: A grumble that this thing, like everything else, can be depressing.
explanation.definitionFit: A lift carries passengers between floors, raising them but also lowering them to the ground.

clue.text: Pats of hall around you sir on the 5

indicators.note: taken as 'the start of', so only the opening letter of the following word is kept
5-down is the lift, so a word riding on it goes upwards, read backwards in a down entry

blocks.note: the setter has the solver addressing himself, so 'you' stands for the first person
taken as written, then carried upwards
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Pats of butter in a hall surround a gentleman riding in the lift.
explanation.walkthrough: I, SIR going up as RIS, and H give IRISH. Pat is an old nickname for an Irishman, like Paddy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pat, short for Patrick, is a traditional nickname for a man from Ireland, so Pats are Irish people.

clue.text: But a different nursery stock yielded its golden fruit

definitions.text: But a different nursery stock yielded its golden fruit

blocks.note: surface reading: young plants raised in a garden nursery

blocks.clueFragment: But a different nursery stock yielded its golden fruit
blocks.note: setter's reading: the nursery rhyme 'I had a little nut tree' bore a silver nutmeg and a golden fruit that grows on a different tree

explanation.surface: A gardener notes that another young tree from the nursery produced a golden crop.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme runs 'I had a little nut tree, nothing would it bear / But a silver nutmeg and a golden pear'.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden fruit in the nursery rhyme is a pear, which naturally grows on its own kind of orchard tree.

clue.text: In this way let her be coming up with an unknown quantity

indicators.note: in a down entry, something coming up is read from the bottom, so the word is turned backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then turned round
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: Someone advises letting a woman be, since she is turning up as an unknown factor.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'coming up' reads upwards, so only the second little word is turned; x, y and z are the algebraic unknowns.
explanation.definitionFit: The formal adverb means by this means or as a result of this, so it replaces 'in this way'.

clue.text: VIP at the Savoy

blocks.note: surface reading: an important guest at the Savoy Hotel in London
setter's reading: the Savoy Theatre, home of Gilbert and Sullivan, whose last opera there has this aristocrat as its title

explanation.surface: A very important person staying at London's grand Savoy Hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Savoy was Gilbert and Sullivan's theatre; their final opera, of 1896, was titled after this ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign of high rank ruling a duchy is a very important personage, and also the title role of that operetta.

clue.text: She shows anger, one's lost love

indicators.note: something lost has gone missing, so a letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: ire is fury
taken as written
love is zero in tennis, a nought shaped like O

explanation.surface: A woman displays her temper because she has lost the man she loved.
explanation.walkthrough: IRE plus ONE without its O gives IRENE.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene is a woman's given name, and a female name can be clued by the pronoun for any woman.

clue.text: Old beer for a stock-getter

blocks.note: first meaning: an eighteenth-century name for porter, drawn from a single cask
second meaning: an uncastrated horse, kept to breed new stock

explanation.surface: Traditional ale offered to a farmer who is buying livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a whole-cask porter bore this name, and a stallion left uncut is called this too, since it can sire foals.

clue.text: Seat of Mars

blocks.note: surface reading: the home or headquarters of the planet or the god
setter's reading: the animal Mars, god of battle, sits on when he rides

explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' suggests a residence; read it as what a rider sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: A charger trained for battle is the mount a god of fighting would ride, hence his seat.

clue.text: Breathing ardency, man with this disguised as duenna ?

definitions.note: the clue's 'man with this disguised as' dresses the second sense up as a costume

blocks.note: first meaning: the fire-breathing monster of legend

blocks.clueFragment: man with this disguised as duenna
blocks.note: second meaning: a fierce, watchful chaperone of a young woman, as a man might play in pantomime

explanation.surface: A passionate suitor gets past the chaperone by dressing up as her.
explanation.walkthrough: A duenna is a Spanish chaperone; the word for a formidable one is the same as the fire-breather.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical beast exhales flames, and a stern, forbidding older woman guarding a girl is called by the same name.

clue.text: They're mean to dogmatize over their years

blocks.note: to aver is to assert positively
long periods of time

explanation.surface: Elderly people are spiteful enough to lay down the law about how old they are.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'over' puts the first piece on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics a mean is one kind of average, so these figures are means.

clue.text: PC Malaprop

blocks.note: surface reading: a police constable called Malaprop
setter's reading: the bumbling constable in Much Ado About Nothing, a man who mangles words just as Mrs Malaprop does

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals misuses long words; Shakespeare's comic constable did the same two centuries earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: The Much Ado watchman is famous for saying the wrong word, so he is a policeman version of Malaprop.

clue.text: Shaved, this cheek

definitions.note: an adjective used in the phrase with cheek, not a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: with no beard or whiskers
second meaning: shameless, as in the phrase for brazen impudence

explanation.surface: A clean-shaven cheek is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheek' looks like part of the face, but it means impudence in a familiar phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally having no hair on one's face, and figuratively undisguised and shameless, as in brazen impudence.

clue.text: Wild cat, lithe as this

indicators.note: wild things are unruly and uncontrolled, so the letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: the two words taken as written

explanation.surface: A wild cat moving with this kind of supple grace.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a supple wild cat is exactly this.
explanation.definitionFit: Fit, strong and agile in movement, which is how a lithe wild cat appears as it prowls.

clue.text: Legal sweeteners, these ?

blocks.note: surface reading: bribes or inducements that are lawful
setter's reading: lawyers' phrase 'by these' for the present document, and gifts are what sweeten people

explanation.walkthrough: Old deeds begin 'Know all men by these', meaning the document in hand, so the word is legal; gifts are sweeteners.
explanation.definitionFit: Gifts given to please people are sweeteners, and in old legal language the word means the document itself.

clue.text: Mass of metal allowed to lie among litter

definitions.note: a phrase for a creature, standing for a noun

blocks.note: a pig is an oblong cast block of iron or lead
let means permitted

explanation.surface: A lump of metal has been permitted to stay lying amid rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' looks like rubbish, but it is a sow's brood.
explanation.definitionFit: A young pig lies among its brothers and sisters, the litter a sow gives birth to.

clue.text: Fox no goose needed to fear

definitions.text: Fox no goose needed to fear

blocks.clueFragment: Fox no goose needed to fear
blocks.note: surface reading: a harmless fox that a farmyard bird would not be scared of
setter's reading: George Fox, founder of the pacifist Quakers, whose members call each other by this name

explanation.walkthrough: Quakers are the Religious Society of Friends, founded by George Fox, and are pacifist; a Quaker would never harm anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A Quaker is formally a member of the Society of Friends, so George Fox was one, and a peaceable one.

clue.text: Books not to upset the bookworm

definitions.note: a verb phrase cluing the third-person verb

blocks.note: first meaning: compilations or summaries in volume form
second meaning: what a stomach does with food so as not to be upset, here a reader taking in books

explanation.surface: Some books are gentle enough not to disturb a keen reader.
explanation.definitionFit: Summaries of law or literature are published volumes, and a reader absorbs and assimilates them the way a stomach handles food.

clue.text: They made ballooning catch on

blocks.note: surface reading: people who made the sport of balloon flight popular
setter's reading: hooks dropped from a balloon to grip the ground and stop it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch on' looks like 'become popular', but means literally take hold of the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: These small multi-pronged anchors were thrown from balloons to snag on trees or earth and bring them to a halt.

clue.text: For you -an unusually ardent spirit

indicators.note: unusually means out of the normal way, so the letters are taken out of their normal order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A toast to someone with a remarkably passionate character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ardent spirit' is an old phrase for strong liquor.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a French brandy liqueur flavoured with fruit kernels, and ardent spirits are distilled strong alcohol.

clue.text: What's the starter doing in the near distance ?

blocks.note: first meaning, cryptic: a race starter is sending runners off
second meaning: the part of the sea visible from shore, as in the phrase about something imminent

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what the official starting a race is up to over there.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors use the word for the stretch of sea visible offshore, hence the idiom for something about to happen.

clue.text: Old man kidded by kid-skin

blocks.note: surface reading: an elderly man teased by a glove or leather
setter's reading: in Genesis, Jacob covered his arms with goatskins to fool his blind father into blessing him

explanation.walkthrough: Jacob's hairy-brother disguise was skins of young goats, so the old father was literally deceived by kid.
explanation.definitionFit: The aged blind patriarch of Genesis was tricked by his son Jacob, who wore goatskins to pass for Esau.

clue.text: Kay with myself and Eve get no further east than this

definitions.text: get no further east than this

indicators.note: going no further means stopping short, so the end of the word is cut off

blocks.note: Kay is how the letter is spelt out
the first person
taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: Three people resolve to travel no further east than a certain place.
explanation.walkthrough: K, I and EVE losing its last letter give KIEV, now usually spelt Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ukrainian capital lay toward the eastern edge of a traveller's Europe, a natural place to stop going eastward.

clue.text: Each single on the Sunset Line

blocks.note: eve is evening, the time of sunset
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Every one-way ticket sold on a railway called the Sunset Line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' looks like a one-way ticket in the railway picture, but it belongs with 'Each' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'every single' means each one without exception, so the two words together stand for the answer.

clue.text: Follow new Ascot fashions

indicators.note: a new version is made over, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: to tail is to shadow someone
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Racegoers keep up with the latest clothes seen at Royal Ascot.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is the royal racecourse where formal morning dress is customary, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal jackets cut away at the front with long skirts behind are particular styles of garment, i.e. fashions.

clue.text: Russian love birds ?

blocks.note: Muscovy is the old name for the principality of Moscow, and so for Russia
duck is a British term of endearment, like love

explanation.surface: Lovebirds, the small parrots, imported from Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: In northern England 'duck' is a friendly way to address someone, like 'love'.
explanation.definitionFit: The large tropical American waterfowl are birds, despite the misleading geographical name.
